title: Toilet Tank Evolution: High-Tank (1880s) to Modern Flush Valve
summary: This Old House host walks through the anatomy of a late-19th-century high-tank toilet and contrasts it with a contemporary tank, illustrating how different components functioned, why older systems were prone to failure, and how modern designs achieve reliable flushing with far less water. The discussion identifies four legacy parts (tank lever, flush valve, fill valve, and copper-walled tank with a copper tank ball float) and traces the transition to a modern flush valve with a flapper, a two-shank overflow, an adjustable fill valve, and a refill tube. The narrative explains the flow path during flush, the role of the siphon jet, and how bowl refill maintains proper water level. It also covers practical maintenance by highlighting two key adjustments—tank lever travel and float level—to ensure a one-flush, water-saving operation, including recommended target water level (about three-quarters of an inch below the overflow).

sections.title: Historical high-tank toilet anatomy
sections.description: Introduction to the 19th-century high-tank toilet, noting its wood tank with copper lining, a weight-driven flush, the four core components (tank lever, flush valve, fill valve, tank ball float), and the basement overflow path when the tank couldn’t stop filling.

sections.title: Early flush valve and lift-system components
sections.description: Discussion of the early, mechanical flush systems with bronze/brass hardware and adjustable lift mechanisms, where the float-and-ball assembly and linkage made reliable seating difficult.

sections.title: Transition to modern flush valve and flapper
sections.description: Contrast with historical designs: the modern flush valve uses a flapper controlled by a tank lever/chain and is paired with two overflow shanks for a more reliable seal and predictable flush.

sections.title: Fill valve, overflow, and refill tube in a modern tank
sections.description: Explains the modern fill valve replacing the old ball, the role of the refill tube in restoring the bowl water level after flush, and how water is directed to the bowl to maintain proper level.

sections.title: Distribute and rinse: flush flow through rim and siphon jet
sections.description: Describes how flush water travels through the rim and siphon jet to scour the bowl, contributing to effective flushing and sanitation.

sections.title: Water efficiency history and current targets
sections.description: Notes the historical trend from approximately 3.5 gallons per flush to contemporary targets around 1.6 gallons, reflecting efficiency improvements over about 150 years.

sections.title: Two practical adjustments for reliable flushing
concepts: target water level near three-quarters inch below overflow
sections.description: Outlines the two common adjustments required for reliable operation: setting the tank lever linkage so the flapper opens enough, and adjusting the float to a water level approximately three-quarters of an inch below the overflow top.

sections.title: Closing remark and universal tank levers
sections.description: A light closing remark noting the ubiquity of tank lever designs and the host’s playful suggestion about museum work.
